(A) True. For equal \((n + l)\) the Madelung rule places the orbital of lower \(n\) lower in energy (e.g. \(3d\) below \(4p\), both with \(n + l = 5\)).
(B) False. As the nuclear charge rises the electron is bound more tightly, so the energy of an orbital of a given subshell DECREASES (becomes more negative) with increasing atomic number.
(C) True. For the same \(l\), size grows with \(n\), so \(2p_{x}\) is smaller than \(3p_{x}\).
(D) False. Radial nodes \(= n - l - 1\): \(5f \rightarrow 1\), \(6s \rightarrow 5\), \(4d \rightarrow 1\), \(5p \rightarrow 3\), \(5d \rightarrow 2\). The \(5d\) orbital does have 2 radial nodes, so the claim that none of them has 2 fails.
Only A and C are true.
authoredSolutions.28: The covalent radius is half the internuclear distance between two like bonded atoms, so for a heteronuclear bond the bond length is the sum of the two covalent radii: \(d_{A-B} = r_{A} + r_{B}\). The overall (end-to-end) length of the molecule adds one atomic radius beyond each nucleus: \(r_{A} + (r_{A} + r_{B}) + r_{B} = 2(r_{A} + r_{B})\). Hence bond length \(= (r_{A} + r_{B})\) and total length \(= 2(r_{A} + r_{B})\).
authoredSolutions.30: Molar heat capacity rises with the number of ways a molecule can store energy. Helium is a monatomic gas with only translational modes, \(C_{p} = \frac{5}{2}R \approx 20.8\) J \(mol^{-1} K^{-1}\). Copper is a monatomic solid obeying the Dulong-Petit limit, \(C \approx 3R \approx 24.4\) J \(mol^{-1} K^{-1}\). Liquid bromine is diatomic and, being a liquid, also stores energy in intermolecular motion, giving the largest value, \(C_{p} \approx 75.7\) J \(mol^{-1} K^{-1}\). Hence Bromine (l) > Copper (s) > Helium (g).
authoredSolutions.31: Starting with amount \(a\) of \(A\), at equilibrium \(A = a - x\), \(B = x\), \(C = x\), so the total amount is \((a - x) + x + x = a + x\). With total pressure \(p\) the partial pressures are \(p_{A} = \frac{a - x}{a + x}p\) and \(p_{B} = p_{C} = \frac{x}{a + x}p\). Therefore \(K_{p} = \frac{p_{B}p_{C}}{p_{A}} = \frac{x^{2}p^{2}/(a + x)^{2}}{(a - x)p/(a + x)} = \frac{x^{2}p}{(a + x)(a - x)} = \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2} - x^{2}} \times p\).

(A) Simple distillation works when the components differ widely in boiling point, so each vaporises essentially separately: A-II.
(B) Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column and is required when the boiling points are close: B-IV.
(C) Steam distillation purifies compounds that are steam volatile and immiscible with water, letting them distil below \(100^{\circ}C\): C-I.
(D) Distillation under reduced pressure lowers the boiling point and is used for liquids that decompose at their normal boiling point (e.g. glycerol): D-III.
So A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.
